description: internal/cli: the shared CLI plumbing. The package had no set at all until #76's CI job made an untested mutant visible as a class of problem; TakeFirst is here because it is what makes `plock unlock <user> --minutes N` parse at all (the flag-order data-loss bug), and Fail/JSON/Keys are here because they are the single implementation of the --json contract every command routes through. HAND-MAINTAINED, like every other set in this directory: there was a scripts/gen-cli-mutations.py that claimed to build this file, and it was deleted (#150) because it emitted 20 mutants into a file that held 21 -- running it silently deleted CI21, which had been appended by hand with #145, while printing `all patterns verified against the source`. Edit this file by appending an entry. Anchor `old` on a statement, never on an aligned composite-literal line: gofmt realigning a literal retires the mutant, the runner reports NOT APPLIED, and the suite stays green.

mutants.note: the "--" separator stops being special, so it falls into the flag branch and swallows the token after it: the documented `unlock -- -x` can no longer name an account called -x, which is the only reason the separator exists

the length check on `after` is dropped, so `TakeFirst` indexes after[0] when the separator is the last token -- `plock unlock --` panics instead of reporting that no account was named. Deliberately NOT cmd.json's TS3, which mutates the SAME line by dropping `!found` instead: that one overwrites a positional already taken (`unlock casey -- anna` acts on anna) and already runs ./internal/cli/ as well as ./cmd/plock/, so re-deriving it here would be one claim counted twice. This is the other half of the condition, and only this package's suite sees it crash.

the adopted token is returned with found=false -- the exact bug the comment above it records: every caller reads a missing positional plus a non-empty fs.Args() as the user making a mistake, so all 17 call sites refuse a valid line at once

the separator is dropped from the remainder instead of copied into it, so flag.Parse sees no separator and `unlock -- casey --minutes 5` adopts casey and then parses --minutes as a flag -- the opposite of what a separator promises (anchored on the following line because `rest = append(rest, a)` also appears in the positional branch below, at the same indent)
a lone "-" stops counting as a positional and is treated as a flag instead
the first positional rule becomes "last one wins", so a second bare token silently replaces the account the operator named

mutants.old: if i+1 < len(args) && flagWantsValue(fs, a, name) {
mutants.note: the bounds check goes, so a trailing flag with no value reads past the end of args -- a panic in the argument parser of a command the operator runs by hand
the lookup is done with the dashes still on, so every known flag looks unknown and inherits the unknown-flag rule -- a boolean flag then eats the following positional
--minutes=5 is no longer recognised as carrying its own value, so it consumes the next token as a value it already has and the positional after it disappears

an unknown flag is assumed valueless instead, which is the direction the comment refuses on purpose: a typo'd flag's value becomes the username, turning a clear complaint about the flag into a confident wrong answer about a child's account

the bool-flag detector never fires, so every flag looks like it takes a value and `--verbose casey` loses casey to the flag -- flag itself never consumes a value after a bool. Mutating the assertion rather than `return !isBool` is deliberate: replacing the return orphans isBool, which is a build failure and not a catch
--json failures print as a human line, so a script reading the failure parses nothing; this is the one implementation of the contract every command routes through
a --json failure exits 0 while stdout is empty, so `plock ... --json` looks like a successful run to anything that checks the exit status
the machine-readable error code is dropped from the failure document, leaving only prose to branch on
HTML escaping is turned back on, so a value containing < or > round-trips as \u003c and the machine-readable format stops being the identity on its own bytes
the alignment column is computed the wrong way round, so labels are not aligned to the widest one seen so far
the blank line before a section is written unconditionally, so a report that starts with a section starts with a stray blank line
a line that already ends in a newline gets a second one, so every table in a report grows a blank row
a negative remaining time is no longer clamped, so a lockout that has already ended renders as a negative wait
Keys stops sorting, and because Go randomises map iteration a machine-readable field built from a map changes between two runs of the same command on the same file

`plock init` stops refusing a weak admin password while the web page still refuses it, which is the drift the alias exists to prevent -- one rule, two surfaces, and the operator's answer depending on which surface they reached for. The constant is aliased rather than copied, so this mutant and I14 attack the same policy from the two ends of that alias. TestInitRefusesAWeakPassword.
